Please install Faiss with conda to make sure that the proper MKL version is installed. 
On intel, we sometimes observe worse MKL perf with nthread = nb cores. Please try 16 threads

> 
It tried out that nthread = nb cores/2 works good for me on another server which has 16 amd processors (both training and query). Thank you so much && I wonder why the performance is bad  with nthread = nb cores :-)

@RongchunYao the performance is likely bad because of the hyper-threading. As you know, typically the hyper-threading is about having two virtual CPU cores sharing the same compute resources of a single real core. And such a sharing is not efficient for linear-algebra ops within Faiss. So, by specifying "nthread = nb codes / 2" you make sure that there's no fight among two virtual CPU cores.
Hope it helps.

title: IndexShards ignores ids in shards
body:
# Summary

<!-- Facebook has a bounty program for the safe disclosure of security bugs. In
those cases, please go through the process outlined on that page and do not
file a public issue. -->

# Platform

<!-- if the question/problem is not platform-specific, please ignore this -->

OS:

Faiss version: 1.7.2

Installed from:

Faiss compilation options: <!-- e.g. using MKL with compile flags ... -->

Running on:
- [x] CPU
- [ ] GPU

Interface: 
- [ ] C++
- [x] Python

# Reproduction instructions

<!-- Please provide specific and comprehensive instructions to reproduce the
described behavior. -->

<!-- Please *do not* post screenshots of logs. They are not searchable. Copy/paste 
the text or make a gist if the text is too bulky. --> 

I did not expect IndexShards to ignore the ID's added to sub-indices, and I don't see how to efficiently work around this. So, I wanted to ask if this is the expected behavior, and - if so - how can I add shards with existing ID's to an IndexShards or IndexBinaryShards?

I see that IndexShards has an add_with_ids, but this would require me to reconstruct an existing index's data. This would be difficult to use because I'm loading each index from disk with the IO_FLAG_MMAP to deal with memory constraints.

Here is a POC of the behavior, the second assert fails, while I expected it to pass:
```
import faiss
import numpy


def make_shard(dimension, data, id_0):
    id_f = id_0 + data.shape[0]
    print(f"Make shard dim. {dimension} data shape {data.shape} ids {id_0}-{id_f - 1}")
    shard = faiss.IndexFlatL2(dimension)
    shard_map = faiss.IndexIDMap(shard)
    ids = numpy.arange(id_0, id_f)
    shard_map.add_with_ids(data, numpy.arange(id_0, id_f))
    return shard_map


def make_sharded_index(dimension, shards):
    index_shards = faiss.IndexShards(dimension)
    for i, shard in enumerate(shards):
        index_shards.add_shard(shard)
    return index_shards


dimension = 32
shard_cnt = 5
shard_sz = 10
kcnt = shard_sz + 1
query_row = 0

data = numpy.random.randn(shard_cnt * shard_sz, dimension).astype(numpy.float32)

all_shards = [make_shard(dimension, data[i:i + shard_sz], i * shard_sz) for i in range(shard_cnt)]

data_query = data[query_row:query_row + 1]

print(f"\nQuery row {query_row} for each shard")
for i, shard in enumerate(all_shards):
    dists, ids = shard.search(data_query, kcnt)
    print(f"shard {i}: dist {dists[0]}")
    print(f"shard {i}: ids {ids[0]}\n")

print(f"Query row {query_row} in sharded index, in created order")
index_shards = make_sharded_index(dimension, all_shards)
dists, ids = index_shards.search(data_query, kcnt)
print(f"shards dist {dists[0]}")
print(f"shards ids {ids[0]}\n")
assert(ids[0][0] == query_row)

print(f"Query row {query_row} in sharded index, out of order")
index_shards = make_sharded_index(dimension, reversed(all_shards))
dists, ids = index_shards.search(data_query, kcnt)
print(f"shards rev dist {dists[0]}")
print(f"shards rev ids {ids[0]}\n")
assert(ids[0][0] == query_row)
```
author: mmaps

comments.body:
IndexShards has flag `successive_ids` to indicate whether the ids of each sub-index is relative to the last index of the previous shard. There is no way when the sub-indexes are built externally to tell if they are successive, and successive_ids is True by default. You should set is explicitly at construction time (or afterwards) with

```
index_shards = IndexShards(dim, False, False) 
```
the first False is to indicate if search should be threaded.

Thanks! This fixes my issue. I had seen `successive_ids`, but didn't realize how it would affect existing ID's until I read your explanation.

If I set exaggerated (like offset +100) ID's in the sub-indexes, its more obvious that IndexShards is picking those up and not counting from 0. So, I wonder why it doesn't ignore `successive_ids` because it doesn't need to number them?

satisfaction_conditions: An explanation of how IndexShards handles IDs from sub-indices
A method to preserve existing IDs when using IndexShards
Clarification on the purpose and behavior of the successive_ids parameter
A solution that works with memory-mapped indices

title: ProductQuantizer  compute_codes get wrong codes when nbits not 8
body:
d = 10
    n = 400000
    cs = 5
    np.random.seed(123)
    x = np.random.random(size=(n, d)).astype('float32')
    testInputs=np.random.random(size=(1, d)).astype('float32')
    print(testInputs)
    pq = faiss.ProductQuantizer(d, cs,6)
    pq.verbose=True
    pq.train(x)
    codes=pq.compute_codes(testInputs)
    #here expect 5 code range from 0-64, but get 4 and also code number not range 0-64
    print(codes.shape)
author: jasstionzyf

comments.body:
This is because the codes are packed into ceil(5 * 6 / 8) = 4 bytes.  
To access the individual codes, use `BitstringReader`: 

```python
bs = faiss.BitstringReader(faiss.swig_ptr(codes[0]), codes.shape[1])
for i in range(cs): 
    print(bs.read(6))  # read 6 bits at a time
````

Admittedly, the `BitstringReader` API could be made more python friendly.
@mdouze   thanks very much!

satisfaction_conditions: An explanation of why the code output differs from the user's expectations
A method to access the individual code values correctly
Code example demonstrating the correct usage pattern

The following code will work on a cpu index, or a GPU index if it has been converted to a CPU index (via `cpuindex = faiss.index_gpu_to_cpu(index)`).

```python
import numpy as np
I = np.empty(n, dtype=np.int64)
I[:] = -1
faiss.search_centroid(
    cpuindex,
    faiss.swig_ptr(query_embs),
    n,
    faiss.swig_ptr(I)
    )
```

However, applying it on a GPU index results in a segfault. I can provide a Colab notebook if necessary?
author: cmacdonald

comments.body: The IVFLib functions such as search_centroid are unfortunately not implemented on the GPU, sorry.
So, to be clear, the best option is to extract the trained centroids from the existing trained index and put them in a new GPU FAISS index?
yes that should work.
and that's what we did. Thanks.

xq[:, 0] += np.arange(nq) / 1000.

index = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d)
co = faiss.GpuMultipleClonerOptions()
co.shard = True
co.useFloat16 = True
index = faiss.index_cpu_to_all_gpus(index, co, ngpu=4)

D, I = index.search(xq, k)

title: IndexIVFFlat on 2M embeddings from FaceNet is giving poor results
body:
# Summary
I am using embeddings computed from the popular FaceNet model. I have calculate about 2.5M embeddings in d=512 and am looking at performance of the `IndexIVFFlat` compared to the simple `Flat` index. Even with large `k` I see flat results in the recall

Running on:
- [ ] GPU

Interface: 
- [ ] Python

# Reproduction instructions
```
xb = np.ascontiguousarray(X[::2][:2*1000*1000])
xq = np.ascontiguousarray(X[1::2][:10*1000])
d = xq.shape[1]

# compute gt
flat_index = faiss.index_factory(d, "Flat")
res = faiss.StandardGpuResources()
index = faiss.index_cpu_to_gpu(res, 0, flat_index, None)
flat_index.train(xb)
flat_index.add(xb)
D, gt = flat_index.search(xq, k)

# try an approximate method
index = faiss.index_factory(d, "IVF<n_centroids>,Flat")
res = faiss.StandardGpuResources()
index = faiss.index_cpu_to_gpu(res, 0, index, None)
index.train(xb)
index.add(xb)

def evaluate(index, xq, gt, k):
    nq = xq.shape[0]
    t0 = time.time()
    D, I = index.search(xq, k)  # noqa: E741
    t1 = time.time()
    recalls = {}
    i = 1
    while i <= k:
        recalls[i] = (I[:, :i] == gt[:, :1]).sum() / float(nq)
        i *= 10

    return (t1 - t0) * 1000.0 / nq, recalls

evaluate(flat_index, xq, gt, 1000)
>>
(2.1849388122558593, 
 {1: 0.99850000000000005, 
  10: 1.0, 
  100: 1.0, 
  1000: 1.0})

evaluate(index, xq, gt, 1000)

>>
(0.038869810104370114,
 {1: 0.35210000000000002,
  10: 0.35289999999999999,
  100: 0.35289999999999999,
  1000: 0.35299999999999998})
```
Notice how the recall is not increasing as k increases.

I have tried many ,<n_centroids>, between  4096 to 20000 and I do not see any improvement. 

### Questions:
1. Is it possible that the data distribution is not conducive to this method? 

2. Am I possibly splitting my query and training set incorrectly?
author: ljstrnadiii

comments.body:
You are only looking in a single IVF list, as `nprobe` is by default 1.

Increase `nprobe` rather than `k`.

of course, merci beaucoup!

I did want to ask about the typical strategy to split your datasets. In some examples I have noticed that you build an xb, xt, xq dataset: one for training, one for adding and the last for query (equivalent to a test set). I am not sure what is the typical split for this field. Do you usually train on xt, add [xt, xb] (or does xb already contain xt?) to the index, and search with xt? It is hard to tell how you have constructed your memmap files. What proportion of the whole dataset is xq, xt and xb typically?

thanks for such a killer project!
